opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
“What can we do to accomplish the works of God?”

It was a reasonable question. They were thinking in terms they understood—effort, action, achievement. Tell us what to do. Give us something to carry out, something measurable, something we can complete.

But His answer didn’t meet them where they expected.

He didn’t hand them a list. He didn’t outline steps or requirements. Instead, He stripped the whole idea down to its core and said:

“The work of God is this: that you believe in the one He has sent.”

There was a pause in that moment—a quiet tension. Because that answer didn’t feel like “work” at all. It felt too simple, almost insufficient. Where were the tasks? The proof? The visible effort?

But that was exactly the point.

They had been thinking that the path to God was something to build—something earned through doing more, trying harder, proving themselves. And in one sentence, He dismantled that entire framework.

The real work, He was saying, isn’t about what you produce. It’s about where you place your trust.  Not a shallow agreement. Not just words. But a deep, internal shift—a decision to rely on Him, to move as if He is truly who He says He is.

That kind of belief isn’t passive. It challenges control. It exposes doubt. It forces a person to stop performing and start depending.

And that’s where everything changes.

Because once that foundation is set—once a person truly believes—then action follows. Not as a way to earn anything, but as a natural response. The doing comes from the believing, not the other way around.

And standing there, hearing His answer, they were left with something far more demanding than a list of tasks.

They were being asked to trust.
